body: There is a small copy-paste ghost here — the feature branch is named `001-gene-regulation` in a project about doubly robust causal estimators, which suggests the spec template was inherited from an unrelated biology project and never fully re-inhabited. That is cosmetic. More substantively, two things deserve a second look. First, User Story 1's acceptance scenario asks that 'the calculated true ATE matches the theoretical expectation within a tolerance of 0.001' for a single simulated draw of N=1000 samples — but the Monte Carlo noise in an empirical ATE computed from one thousand observations will typically be orders of magnitude larger than 0.001. The true ATE must be computed analytically (or by integration over the covariate distribution), not estimated from a finite sample, or this acceptance test will fail even in a perfectly correct implementation. Second, the framing of the research question — whether dual-misspecification bias is 'merely additive' versus 'amplified' — brushes against a known result: the AIPW bias term has the form E[(1 − e/ê)(m̂ − m)], a product of the two errors, so some interaction is guaranteed by construction, not a discovery. Kang and Schafer (2007), cited in spirit via the related work, already characterized this. The spec's meta-regression over categorical misspecification types (FR-005) can rank which pairings produce large products, which is genuinely useful, but the spec never defines the additive baseline against which 'amplification' is judged — SC-002 tests an interaction coefficient against zero without stating what the main-effect-only model would predict for bias magnitude. Clarifying that baseline would make the 'danger zones' claim falsifiable rather than tautological. The clipping of propensity scores to [0.01, 0.99] is sensible, though it slightly muddies the 'doubly robust' validation in US-2, since clipping is itself a form of propensity misspecification in finite samples.
